title: The Man Spectrum
author: Renn, Aaron
summary: Aaron Renn argues that contemporary masculinity discourse is too narrow, forcing men into either a blue-collar/outdoorsman archetype or a rejected 'toxic' label, and uses the Apostle Paul as an extended case study of how wide the legitimate range of masculine expression actually is. Working through Paul's life — elite social status, singular mission, intellectual and spiritual depth, talent development of proteges like Timothy, and even self-described nurturing tenderness — Renn shows a single historical figure embodying traits our culture currently splits into 'masculine' and 'feminine' categories. He adds King David as a complementary example of artistic sensibility coexisting with martial and political virtues. The essay's stated aim is practical: young men need a spectrum wide enough to include the elite as well as the working-class, the nurturing as well as the physically tough, so that those who don't fit a narrow stereotype aren't told they've failed at manhood, while still holding a real, non-negotiable standard (mission, strength, courage) that anchors the category.
points: Uses the Apostle Paul as a single case study showing elite status, intellectual depth, spiritual life, mentorship, and self-described nurturing tenderness can all coexist within one 'man's man.'
Argues a workable definition of masculinity must be capacious enough to include both elite/urban and working-class/rural men without treating either as less authentic.
Claims mission and purpose — something worth sacrificing comfort for — matters more to manhood than the more commonly cited markers of marriage and fatherhood.
Names generational talent development (raising up and passing the baton to younger men) as a duty men owe, and one society has largely failed at.
Insists the goal isn't infinite elasticity — strength, courage, and pursuit of higher goods remain close to non-negotiable even as the acceptable expressions of masculinity widen.
quotes: Not every man needs to be about bourbon, hunting, Carhartt jackets, and Super Duties. I love bacon, IPAs, deadlifting, and home improvement projects as much as the next guy, but the reality is that masculinity has a much broader range than we think of it today.

With many young American men struggling, masculinity as likely to be described as "toxic" as anything good in the media, and a variety of dodgy online influencers who are actually leaning into the idea that toxic masculinity is good, it's important for our society to put forth a positive, aspirational, attractive vision of masculinity that men actually want and can imagine themselves being part of.

The lesson from Paul is that any positive vision of manhood must be capacious enough to include men from every socio-economic and occupational class. It shouldn't be out of reach for the poor, but neither should being rich or elite be seen as incompatible with being a "real man.

Not everyone needs to act like a monk, but men need a mission, a purpose to pursue, a sense that they matter. They need to have something for which they would sacrifice their comfort or in some cases even their lives if necessary.
The lesson here is that it is incumbent on men to build up the next generation under them and successfully pass the baton. This is something we've failed miserably at as a society.

Today, a relational orientation and nurturing style are seen as hallmarks of a feminine style. It's true that women tend to be stronger in these traits, but the lesson here is that these are tools men can have in their repertoire as well.

They need a society that provides a man spectrum they can put themselves on, one also with a standard to meet and excellences to aspire to, and which provides validation and honor to those who measure up to that.
